newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish PM stirs political storm during China trip.
newsitem.headline: Swedish PM stirs political storm during China trip.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson found himself at the centre of a political storm on Tuesday for making what was viewed here as favourable comments on China's political stability during a visit to Beijing.
"To me it's striking what political stability means for economic development when you look at the Chinese example," Persson said as he met premier Jiang Zemin on Monday.

Expressing outrage at the comments, which were seen as condoning China's human rights record, opposition politicians demanded that Persson should be summoned before the nation's Foreign Policy Committee to explain himself.
Liberal Party leader Maria Leissner demanded that Persson retract his comments -- or face a vote of no confidence after just eight months in office.

"A Swedish prime minister who travels to the world's biggest and bloodiest dictatorship and describes its stability as an advantage ... does not represent Swedish foreign policy in a proper manner," Leissner told Swedish daily Svenska Dagbladet.

But the Liberals represent just seven percent of the Swedish parliament, and Leissner's call to oust Persson was not taken up by the Conservatives and Christian Democrats who control about 22 percent and eight percent respectively of the 349 seats.
But the two parties did back a call for an extraordinary session of the Foreign Policy Committee to be convened when Persson returns to Sweden later this week.
"It's reasonable to start with a Foreign Policy Committee hearing to give Persson the chance to explain himself," Moderate party secretary Gunnar Hokmark told Swedish news agency TT.
Persson, on a four-day visit to China and Hong Kong, refused to retract his comments.
"The fact is that China has good economic development, but this does not exempt them from criticism about their human rights. I pointed this out as well," Persson told Swedish television on Tuesday.
To the tabloid newspaper Aftonbladet, he commented: "I do not regret it at all.
"What I've done is to bring up a discussion over economic development and political stability. I'm surprised over the Liberals' reactions...and cheap point scoring."

Persson, whose Social Democrats control about 46 percent of parliament, said a vote of no confidence was the strongest instrument available in parliament. "It should be saved until there really are grounds to use it," he said.
